title: We Need More Than a Child Tax Credit to Boost Education Outcomes
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler uses the launch of the expanded child tax credit to argue that cash transfers alone will not close the achievement gap. She points to a Brookings study showing that maternal education, not income, was the one factor that gave poor children a kindergarten-readiness edge over wealthier peers, which suggests that knowledge and vocabulary transmitted by educated parents is what matters. Because schools cannot replace that home advantage entirely, she contends they must do far more than they do now. Her diagnosis is twofold: unsystematic phonics instruction that leaves many poor children guessing at words, and a comprehension-skills approach that crowds out knowledge-building subjects like science and social studies. The remedy she proposes costs no new money: better teacher training and a knowledge-rich curriculum starting in kindergarten.
points: The Brookings data (91% of poor children with highly educated mothers ready for kindergarten versus 84% of wealthier peers) shows parental education, not income, is the decisive factor.
Money helps struggling families but cannot substitute for the academic knowledge and vocabulary that educated parents pass on.
Poorly systematic phonics instruction disproportionately harms low-income children, who end up guessing at words instead of decoding them.
Skills-based comprehension practice on easy books, plus the sidelining of science and social studies, widens knowledge gaps that schools should be closing.
The fix is within existing K-12 spending: better teacher preparation and curriculum built around academic knowledge from kindergarten.
quotes: Unfortunately, though, giving families more money is unlikely to significantly narrow the education-outcome gap. Yes, family income and wealth is highly correlated with educational achievement.

But the Brookings study included a striking statistic: poor children whose mothers had at least a BA degree were actually more likely to be ready for kindergarten than kids in the same category from more affluent families. Specifically, 91% of the poor children with highly educated mothers were prepared, compared to only 84% of their more affluent peers.

Why would that be? Most likely, because parents with more education expose their children to more sophisticated concepts and vocabulary, providing them with the kind of knowledge that enables academic success.

Virtually all equity-focused policy prescriptions are overlooking what goes on in classrooms between kindergarten and twelfth grade, perhaps because previous attempts to improve the system haven’t worked. That’s a huge mistake.

One big part of the problem is our failure to teach foundational reading skills like phonics in a way that ensures all children will acquire them. Educators often believe they’re teaching phonics, but their approach is so unsystematic that many kids end up guessing at words rather than sounding them out—and those kids are disproportionately from the lower end of the socioeconomic spectrum.

Throughout elementary school and often beyond, students spend many hours every week practicing supposed skills like “finding the main idea” on books that are easy for them to read on their own. Subjects that could build academic knowledge and vocabulary, like social studies and science, have been marginalized or eliminated from the curriculum, especially where scores are low.

But we shouldn’t expect money alone to compensate for lack of parental education, or break the cycle of multi-generational poverty. For that, we need to provide better teacher training and the kind of curriculum that focuses on building academic knowledge, beginning in kindergarten.
